lines.text: The last topic established that a committed change is durable in the log before the page itself is.
But a log nobody ever trims would mean a crash has to replay the engine's entire history, from the very beginning.
Something marks a far more recent, trustworthy point to start from instead.
That something is a checkpoint's own redo record, read directly off a live cluster rather than assumed.
It names the exact position recovery would resume from if a crash happened this very instant.
And the live distance behind that position is exactly how much work a crash right now would force.
Checkpoint more often, and there's genuinely less work to redo after a crash — that part is the clear win.
But the same documentation names a real cost sitting right next to it.
With the page-tear defense turned on, checkpointing more often also means logging a full page copy more often.

lines.text: Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
A disk doesn't write an entire page in one physical step — it lands in several smaller physical pieces, one after another.
If a crash happens partway through, why would the whole page need logging, rather than just the change being made?
It's not a format limitation, and it's not about saving space either — it's a physical problem.
Some of those smaller physical pieces can land while others never do, leaving a page that's part old and part new.
Applying an ordinary change on top of that mixed-up state could still produce something wrong, so only a full, known-good copy of the page can safely repair whatever a crash left behind.
Here's that trade-off shown directly, not just argued for.
Checkpointing after every single one of ten identical rounds of change, measured directly against a real cluster: a very large number of full-page copies logged.
And the live distance a crash would need to replay, kept down to something small.
The identical rounds of change, measured again, but checkpointed only once at the very start instead.
Far fewer full-page copies logged this time — a small fraction of the earlier count.
But the live distance a crash would need to replay has grown far larger instead, the trade-off flipped in the opposite direction.
A completely different piece of this same topic is worth naming directly.

A well-known recovery method, named from its own original paper, describes three separate passes: figuring out what was happening, redoing everything, and then undoing the transactions that never finished.
This sandbox's own engine describes only one of those passes — redo — because a change's own transaction status decides what's visible, with nothing left to physically undo.
The exact same log this whole topic measures turns out to get reused for three more jobs entirely.
Stop replaying it early instead of running it to the end, and that's a point-in-time recovery.

Ship the identical bytes to another machine that keeps applying them continuously, and that's physical replication. Decode those same bytes into row-level changes instead, and that's the basis of logical decoding.
Pulling the whole topic back together.
A checkpoint's own redo record, naming the real starting point for recovery.

A real, measured trade-off, pulling two real costs in opposite directions by a huge margin each. One engine that redoes only, deciding visibility by a change's own status rather than physically undoing anything. And the identical log, reused for three more jobs entirely.
One closing scenario, worth reasoning through before the explanation lands.
A system claims instant crash recovery no matter how long it's been running, without ever mentioning anything like a checkpoint.
Before believing that claim, what would actually have to be true underneath it?
It can't really be true as stated, and the giveaway isn't about redo versus undo at all — that's a separate question this topic already settled.

Any crash-recovery claim that doesn't grow with how long a system has been running has to be capping how far back it looks somehow, and that capping is exactly the job this topic's own checkpoint does.
A claim of instant recovery with no stated bound at all is either marketing, or it's quietly hiding a checkpoint-equivalent under a different name.
